title: Sound; Stationary waves and harmonics; Boundary behavior of waves
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics 2 (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: W17-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; W10-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; W17-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; W19-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: W10-1#N.8b, W17-1#N.4, W19-1#N.3, W10-1#N.10, W19-1#N.5, W19-1#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Wavelength
items.clue: Equal to v/f, so it changes when the wave passes into a new medium.

items.label: Node
items.clue: Point where the amplitude is zero at all times; the next one is λ/2 away.

items.label: Frequency
items.clue: Set by the source, so it stays the same when the wave passes into a new medium.

items.label: Reflected wave
items.clue: Part sent back into the first medium at a boundary, keeping the incident speed.

questions.stem: Pipe X is open at both ends. The frequencies at which standing sound waves form in it are 400 Hz, 800 Hz, 1200 Hz, and so on. One end of pipe X is then closed, with its length and the air inside unchanged. What is now the second-lowest frequency at which a standing wave can form in the pipe?

A student at one end of a long steel railway track puts an ear to the rail. At the other end, 1.0 km away, the rail is struck once with a hammer. The student hears two separate sounds, 0.20 s and 2.9 s after the blow. Which conclusion do these observations support?

options.text: Sound is slowed by closely packed particles: the first sound came through the air.
Sound has one fixed speed, so the second sound was an echo of the first sound.
Sound travels faster in steel than in air: the first sound came through the rail.
The blow pushed steel along the rail to the ear, so the sound through the rail came first.

questions.stem: Predict first. Sound from a loudspeaker in air reaches the surface of a swimming pool, and sound travels on into the water. Which property of the sound is the same in the water as in the air?

options.text: The distance between its adjacent compressions
The distance it travels in each second
The amount of energy it carries each second
The number of oscillations it makes each second

questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode. The tension in the string is then increased to four times its original value, with the length and the string unchanged. By what factor does the frequency of the fundamental change?

options.text: ×½

questions.stem: Predict first. A light string is tied to a heavy string under the same tension, so waves travel more slowly on the heavy string. An upright pulse (displaced upward) travels along the light string toward the knot. Which claim about the reflected pulse, with its reasoning, is correct?

options.text: It is upright, as the transmitted pulse travels more slowly.
It is inverted, as the transmitted pulse travels more slowly.
It is inverted, as a reflection flips a pulse at any boundary.
There is none, as the whole pulse passes into the heavy string.

questions.stem: At night, a person in a brightly lit room sees a faint reflection of the room in the window, while people outside can see into the room through the same window. What does this show?

options.text: Glass reflects light only at night; by day it transmits all the light.
Glass transmits all the light; the faint image is light scattered by dust.
Light going from air into glass is reflected; light going from glass into air is transmitted.
At each glass surface, part of the light is reflected, part transmitted.

questions.explanation: The speed of light changes at the boundary, so the wave splits: a small part is reflected (the faint image) and most is transmitted (seen from outside).
